messages.content: Write a customer case study about a company that adopted a continuous delivery platform and now deploys more often. Around 250 words.

output:
Here's a draft. The company and numbers are invented — swap in your real customer's details before it goes anywhere public.

---

## Marlow Retail Systems cut its release cycle from three weeks to a day

For six years, Marlow shipped on Thursdays. The release window opened at 8 p.m., three engineers stayed late, and by midnight someone usually had a rollback script open. "We batched a month of work into one night," says Priya Ntembe, who runs platform engineering. "Then we spent Friday finding out which of the forty changes broke checkout."

The batching was the problem, not the people. Every release carried so many changes that a failure took hours to trace back to its cause. So the team stopped batching.

They moved to a continuous delivery platform in the spring of 2024, starting with one service — the pricing API, chosen because it had decent test coverage and a small blast radius. Every merge to main now builds, runs the suite, and rolls out to five percent of traffic. If error rates climb above baseline, the rollout reverses itself without anyone paging.

Fourteen months in, Marlow deploys 38 times a week across 22 services, up from roughly one. Change failure rate fell from 11 percent to 3. The Thursday window is gone.

The gains weren't free. Two engineers spent most of a quarter writing the tests and health checks the pipeline depends on, and a few teams resisted giving up manual approval gates until they watched an automated rollback catch a bad migration in ninety seconds.

"We don't talk about releases anymore," Ntembe says. "We talk about what we're building. The shipping part got boring, which is what you want."
